fields.title: Malachi
fields.subtitle: Malakhi, “My messenger”
fields.description: The last of the twelve Minor Prophets and the last book of the Old Testament, spoken to the people of Judah a few generations after the temple was rebuilt, when worship had become a chore and faithfulness seemed to bring no reward. It is a book of arguments: God says “I have loved you”, and the people ask, “In what way have you loved us?” Blind and lame offerings, priests who cause many to stumble, broken marriages and withheld tithes are answered by a God who says “I am the LORD, and I do not change”, who keeps a book of remembrance for those who fear him, and who promises a messenger to clear the way, a refiner’s fire, the sun of righteousness rising, “bringing healing in its wings”, and Elijah the prophet before the great day of the LORD. Set out line by line, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Malachi about?
qa.answer: A people who had grown weary of God. After the exile, with the temple rebuilt, the priests offered blemished sacrifices, men broke faith with their wives, tithes went unpaid, and many said it was useless to serve God. Malachi answers in six disputes in which God makes a statement, the people question it, and God replies. The book ends by calling the people to remember the law of Moses and promising that Elijah the prophet will come before the great day of the LORD.

qa.question: Who wrote Malachi, and when?
qa.answer: The book is “the word of the LORD to Israel through Malachi” (1:1). The name means “my messenger”, and scholars differ over whether it is the prophet’s personal name or a title taken from 3:1; the ancient Greek translation read it as “his messenger”, and one Jewish tradition identified the author as Ezra. The book mentions a governor and a working temple, and deals with the same problems as Ezra and Nehemiah, so it is usually dated to the Persian period, around the middle of the fifth century BC.

qa.question: What does “I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated” mean?
qa.answer: In Malachi 1:2–3 God answers the people’s doubt of his love by pointing to the different histories of Jacob’s descendants, Israel, and Esau’s, Edom, which lay in ruins. In the language of covenant, “love” and “hate” here mean choosing one to carry the promise and not the other. Paul quotes the words in Romans 9:13 in his argument that God’s promises rest on his choice rather than human birth or effort. Christians have long disagreed about how far that argument extends to individual salvation.

qa.question: Who is the messenger in Malachi 3:1?
qa.answer: God promises to send “my messenger” to clear the way, after which “the Lord you are seeking will come to his temple”. Malachi 4:5 names this forerunner as Elijah the prophet. The New Testament identifies him with John the Baptist: Mark 1:2 quotes the verse at the start of John’s ministry, Jesus applies it to John in Matthew 11:10, and an angel says John will go ahead of the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). The Lord who comes to his temple is, for the New Testament, Jesus.

qa.question: Why does Malachi have four chapters in English Bibles but three in Hebrew?
qa.answer: The difference is only in numbering. Hebrew Bibles count the last six verses as Malachi 3:19–24; English Bibles, following the Latin tradition, make them a separate chapter 4. This edition uses the English numbering. In synagogue reading, the verse promising Elijah (4:5 in English) is read again after the last verse, so that the prophets do not end on a word of destruction.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
See, I am sending my messenger, and he will clear the way ahead of me. Then suddenly the Lord you are seeking will come to his temple; the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, is coming, says the LORD of Armies.

— Malachi 3:1

Malachi is the last book of the Old Testament in Christian Bibles, and it ends looking forward. Its final verses promise a messenger, the prophet Elijah, who will come before the great day of the LORD. Then the prophetic voice falls silent for some four hundred years, until a man dressed like Elijah appears in the wilderness by the Jordan. The Gospels open by saying that Malachi’s promise has begun to come true.

The name Malachi means “my messenger”, the very words used in the promise of 3:1. Some think it was the prophet’s name; others think it is a title, taken from that verse, for a prophet whose name we do not know. The ancient Greek translation reads the first verse as “by the hand of his messenger”, and one Jewish tradition identified the author with Ezra. Either way, the book is about a messenger, and about the God who sends him.

Its place in the Bible gives it extra weight. In the Hebrew Bible, Malachi closes the Book of the Twelve, the single scroll that holds the Minor Prophets, and the Writings follow, ending in most printed editions with Chronicles. Most Christian Bibles put the prophets last, so that Malachi stands at the very end of the Old Testament, its promise of a coming messenger facing the first page of Matthew.

The time

Malachi gives no date, but the book’s world is clear. The temple has been rebuilt, for priests are offering sacrifices on its altar. Judah is ruled by a “governor”, as it was under Persia. And the problems Malachi addresses are the very ones that Ezra and Nehemiah faced in the middle of the fifth century BC: careless priests, Jewish men marrying women who worshipped other gods, and tithes not brought, so that the Levites had to leave the temple to work their fields (Nehemiah 13). Most scholars date Malachi to that time, perhaps around 460–430 BC.

It was a time of disappointment. Haggai and Zechariah had promised that the glory of the new temple would be greater than the old, that the nations would come, that the LORD would live in Jerusalem. Two or three generations later, the temple stood, but nothing seemed to have changed. The people were not rebellious so much as tired. Worship had become a chore; faithfulness seemed to bring no reward. “What a burden this is!” they said of the altar, and sniffed at it.

A book of arguments

Malachi is built as a series of disputes. Again and again God makes a statement, the people answer with a question, “Yet you ask, ‘In what way…?’”, and God replies. It reads like a court case, or a quarrel within a family, and both are fitting.

  • 1:2–5: “I have loved you.” “In what way have you loved us?”
  • 1:6–2:9: priests who despise God’s name. “In what way have we despised your name?”
  • 2:10–16: faithlessness. To one another, and to “the wife you married in your youth”.
  • 2:17–3:5: “Where is the God of justice?” The Lord will come to his temple.
  • 3:6–12: “Return to me.” “In what way shall we return?”
  • 3:13–4:3: “It is useless to serve God.” The book of remembrance and the coming day.
  • 4:4–6: Moses and Elijah. A closing charge and a promise.

“I have loved you”

The book begins where all God’s dealings with his people begin:

I have loved you, says the LORD. Yet you ask, “In what way have you loved us?” Was Esau not Jacob’s brother? declares the LORD. Even so, I loved Jacob, but Esau I hated. I have turned his mountains into a wasteland and left his inheritance to the jackals of the desert.

— Malachi 1:2–3

The people doubt God’s love because their lives are hard. God answers by pointing to Edom, the nation descended from Jacob’s brother, now in ruins. In the language of covenant, to “love” Jacob and “hate” Esau means to choose one to carry the promise and not the other, as Genesis tells; in Malachi it concerns two peoples, Israel and Edom, rather than God’s feelings toward individuals. Paul quotes the line in Romans 9:13 as part of his argument that God’s promises rest on his choosing, not on human birth or effort. Christians have long disagreed about how far that argument reaches, but Malachi’s own point is plain: Israel’s existence is evidence that God has loved it.

Blind and lame offerings

The longest dispute is with the priests. They bring blind, lame and sick animals to the altar, things they would never dare offer a human ruler:

When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not wrong? When you offer animals that are lame or sick, is that not wrong? Just try offering such a thing to your governor! Would he be pleased with you or receive you kindly? says the LORD of Armies.

— Malachi 1:8

God would rather someone shut the temple doors than go on lighting “useless fires on my altar”. And then, in the middle of the rebuke, comes one of the widest horizons in the Old Testament:

From where the sun rises to where it sets, my name is great among the nations. In every place incense is offered to my name, and pure offerings, because my name is great among the nations, says the LORD of Armies.

— Malachi 1:11

The early church read this verse as a promise of worship among the Gentiles; the Didache and Justin Martyr both applied it to the Christian Eucharist. Malachi sets it beside a picture of what a priest should be: his covenant with Levi was “one of life and peace”, “True instruction was in his mouth”, and “he turned many back from sin”, “For a priest’s lips should preserve knowledge”.

The verse goes on to give the priest a title: “he is the messenger of the LORD of Armies.” It is the same word as the prophet’s name. The priests were meant to be God’s messengers, carrying his instruction to the people. Because they have “caused many to stumble”, God will send another messenger of his own.

Faithful to one another

The third dispute begins with two questions: “Do we not all have one father? Was it not one God who created us?” Then why break faith with one another? Malachi names two ways. Men of Judah were marrying women who worshipped other gods, “the daughter of a foreign god”, and some were divorcing the wives of their youth. They wept at the altar because God no longer accepted their offerings, and asked why:

Yet you ask, “Why?” Because the LORD was a witness between you and the wife you married in your youth. You have broken faith with her, though she is your partner and your wife by covenant.

— Malachi 2:14

The Hebrew of the next two verses is among the hardest in the prophets. This translation reads verse 16 as “For I hate divorce, says the LORD”; others read it as a saying about the man who divorces his wife out of dislike, who “covers his garment with violence”. Either way, the passage stands firmly with the wife who has been wronged, and calls marriage a covenant of which God himself is witness.

The messenger and the refiner

The people complain that God does not care about justice: “Where is the God of justice?” He answers with the promise at the head of this introduction. A messenger will clear the way, and then the Lord they are seeking will come suddenly to his temple. But they should be careful what they ask for:

But who can bear the day of his coming? Who can hold their ground when he appears? For he will be like a refiner’s fire and like the soap of those who wash clothes. He will sit like one who refines and purifies silver; he will purify the descendants of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, so that they will belong to the LORD and bring offerings in righteousness.

— Malachi 3:2–3

He comes first to purify the priests, and then to judge everyone who wrongs the weak: those who cheat hired workers of their wages, oppress widows and orphans, and deny justice to foreigners. Mark’s Gospel opens by quoting Malachi’s promise together with Isaiah’s, and Jesus himself said of John the Baptist, “This is the man of whom Scripture says, ‘I am sending my messenger ahead of you’” (Matthew 11:10).

“I do not change”

The fifth dispute rests on a single verse:

I am the LORD, and I do not change; that is why you, descendants of Jacob, have not been destroyed.

— Malachi 3:6

The people have changed, again and again, since the days of their ancestors. God has not, and that is the only reason they still exist. So he calls them back, “Return to me, and I will turn to you again”, and when they ask how, he names their tithes. “Will a mortal rob God?” Then he makes a rare invitation: bring the full tithe, “Put me to the test in this”, and see if he will not “open the windows of heaven for you”.

The book of remembrance

The last dispute is the saddest. Some had decided, “It is useless to serve God.” The arrogant prosper and evildoers get away with it. But not everyone thought so:

Then those who feared the LORD talked with one another, and the LORD listened and heard them. A book of remembrance was written in his presence about those who feared the LORD and honored his name.

— Malachi 3:16

God calls them “my special treasure”. And he promises a day that will make the difference between the righteous and the wicked plain again: a day “blazing like a furnace” for the arrogant, but for those who revere his name, a sunrise:

But for you who revere my name, the sun of righteousness will rise, bringing healing in its wings. You will go out leaping like calves let out of the stall.

— Malachi 4:2

Christians have sung of Christ as that rising sun ever since: “Hail the Sun of Righteousness”, in Charles Wesley’s Christmas hymn.

How to read Malachi

Malachi is short, and it reads quickly. Notice the pattern of the disputes, and listen for your own voice in the people’s questions: “In what way have you loved us?” “What have we said against you?” They are the questions of people who have not left God, but have stopped expecting much from him. Then read it with the opening chapters of Matthew, Mark and Luke beside it, where the messenger finally arrives.

When Malachi is read in synagogues, verse 4:5 is read again after the last verse, so that the book, and the prophets, do not end on the word “destruction” but on the promise of Elijah. It is a good instinct. Malachi’s last word is a warning, but its last hope is a coming.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Most of Malachi is set out here one line per line, as poetry. A few of the translation’s choices are worth knowing.

“The LORD of Armies.” This title, which older Bibles render “the LORD of hosts”, appears twenty-four times in Malachi’s fifty-five verses, almost always as the signature on God’s words: “says the LORD of Armies”.

The people’s questions. The repeated question of the disputes is rendered “In what way…?”, so that the pattern can be heard each time it comes.

Chapter 4. In Hebrew Bibles, Malachi has three chapters, and the last six verses are numbered 3:19–24. This edition follows English Bibles and prints them as chapter 4.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Malachi 1
fields.body_html:
I have loved you

An oracle: the word of the LORD to Israel
through Malachi.
I have loved you, says the LORD.
Yet you ask, “In what way have you loved us?”
Was Esau not Jacob’s brother? declares the LORD.
Even so, I loved Jacob,
but Esau I hated.
I have turned his mountains into a wasteland
and left his inheritance to the jackals of the desert.
Edom may say, “We have been crushed, but we will rebuild the ruins.”
But the LORD of Armies says this: They may build, but I will tear down.
They will be called the Land of Wickedness,
the people with whom the LORD is angry forever.
You will see it with your own eyes,
and you will say, “Great is the LORD,
even beyond the borders of Israel!”
A son honors his father, and a servant honors his master.
If I am a father, where is the honor due to me? If I am a master, where is the respect due to me? says the LORD of Armies to you priests who despise my name.
Yet you ask, “In what way have we despised your name?”
You offer defiled food on my altar.
Yet you ask, “In what way have we defiled you?”
By saying,
“The table of the LORD may be despised.”
When you offer blind animals in sacrifice, is that not wrong?
When you offer animals that are lame or sick, is that not wrong?
Just try offering such a thing to your governor! Would he be pleased with you or receive you kindly?
says the LORD of Armies.
So now, plead with God to be gracious to us!
With such offerings from your hands,
will he show favor to any of you? says the LORD of Armies.
If only one of you would close the temple doors
and stop you from lighting useless fires on my altar!
I have no pleasure in you, says the LORD of Armies,
and I will not accept an offering from your hands.
From where the sun rises to where it sets, my name is great among the nations.
In every place incense is offered to my name, and pure offerings,
because my name is great among the nations,
says the LORD of Armies.
But you profane it
by saying, “The Lord’s table is defiled,
and the food on it can be despised.”
You say, “What a burden this is!” and you sniff at it in contempt, says the LORD of Armies.
You bring animals that were stolen, or lame or sick,
and these you bring as your offering!
Should I accept that from your hands? says the LORD.

Cursed is the cheat who has a sound male in their flock and vows to give it,
but then sacrifices to the Lord an animal with a blemish!
I am a great King, says the LORD of Armies,
and my name is feared among the nations.

fields.title: Malachi 2
fields.body_html:
A warning to the priests

And now, you priests, this command is for you.
If you will not listen, and if you will not resolve to give glory to my name, says the LORD of Armies,
I will send the curse on you
and turn your blessings into curses.
In fact, I have already cursed them,
because you have not taken this to heart.
I am about to rebuke your descendants,
and I will smear dung on your faces,
the dung of your festival sacrifices,
and you will be carried off with it.
Then you will know that I have sent you this command
so that my covenant with Levi may stand,
says the LORD of Armies.
My covenant with him was one of life and peace,
and I gave them to him so that he would revere me, and he did revere me
and stood in awe of my name.
True instruction was in his mouth,
and nothing wrong was found on his lips.
In peace and uprightness he walked with me,
and he turned many back from sin.
For a priest’s lips should preserve knowledge,
and people should look to him for instruction,
because he is the messenger of the LORD of Armies.
But you have turned from the way
and caused many to stumble by your instruction.
You have ruined the covenant of Levi,
says the LORD of Armies.
So I in turn have made you contemptible and lowly in the eyes of all the people,
since you have not kept to my ways
and you show favoritism in your instruction.

Unfaithful to one another

Do we not all have one father?
Was it not one God who created us?
So why are we unfaithful to one another,
profaning the covenant of our ancestors?
Judah has been unfaithful,
and a detestable practice has been carried out in Israel and in Jerusalem.
Judah has profaned what is holy to the LORD, what he loves,
by marrying the daughter of a foreign god.
May the LORD cut off from the tents of Jacob
every man who does this, whoever he may be,
even if he brings an offering
to the LORD of Armies.

The wife of your youth

And here is another thing you do:
you flood the LORD’s altar with tears,
weeping and groaning,
because he no longer looks on your offerings
or accepts them gladly from your hands.
Yet you ask, “Why?”
Because the LORD was a witness between you and the wife you married in your youth. You have broken faith with her,
though she is your partner and your wife by covenant.
Did he not make them one, with a portion of spirit in their union?
And why one?
Because he was seeking godly offspring.
So guard yourselves in your spirit,
and let no one be unfaithful to the wife of his youth.
For I hate divorce, says the LORD, the God of Israel,
and I hate it when a man covers his garment with violence,
says the LORD of Armies.
So guard yourselves in your spirit, and do not be unfaithful.

Where is the God of justice?

You have wearied the LORD with your words.
Yet you ask, “In what way have we wearied him?”
When you say, “All who do evil are good in the LORD’s sight, and he is pleased with them,”
or by asking, “Where is the God of justice?”

fields.title: Malachi 3
fields.body_html:
The coming messenger

See, I am sending my messenger,
and he will clear the way ahead of me.
Then suddenly the Lord you are seeking will come to his temple; the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, is coming,
says the LORD of Armies.
But who can bear the day of his coming?
Who can hold their ground when he appears?
For he will be like a refiner’s fire
and like the soap of those who wash clothes.
He will sit like one who refines and purifies silver;
he will purify the descendants of Levi and refine them
like gold and silver,
so that they will belong to the LORD
and bring offerings in righteousness.
Then the offering of Judah and Jerusalem will be pleasing to the LORD,
as it was in days gone by,
in years long past.
I will come near to you for judgment.
I will be quick to testify against sorcerers and adulterers
and those who swear falsely,
against those who cheat hired workers of their wages, who oppress widows and orphans and deny justice to foreigners, and who do not fear me,
says the LORD of Armies.
I am the LORD, and I do not change;
that is why you, descendants of Jacob, have not been destroyed.
Ever since the days of your ancestors you have strayed from my statutes and failed to keep them.
Return to me, and I will turn to you again,
says the LORD of Armies.
Yet you ask, “In what way shall we return?”
Will a mortal rob God? But you are robbing me.
Yet you ask, “In what way do we rob you?”
In tithes and offerings.
You are under a curse,
because you are robbing me,
the whole nation of you.
Bring the full tithe into the storehouse, so that there will be food in my house.
Put me to the test in this,
says the LORD of Armies,
and see if I do not open the windows of heaven for you
and pour out on you a blessing until you have more than enough.
I will rebuke the devourer for your sake,
so that it will not destroy the crops of your land,
and your vines in the field will not fail to bear fruit,
says the LORD of Armies.
Then all the nations will call you blessed,
because you will be a delightful land,
says the LORD of Armies.

A book of remembrance

You have said harsh things against me, says the LORD.
Yet you ask,
“What have we said against you?”
You have said, “It is useless to serve God.
What do we gain by keeping his requirements
and walking around like mourners
before the LORD of Armies?
So now we count the arrogant as blessed.
Evildoers not only prosper;
they put God to the test and get away with it.”
Then those who feared the LORD talked with one another,
and the LORD listened and heard them.
A book of remembrance was written in his presence
about those who feared the LORD and honored his name.
They will be mine, says the LORD of Armies,
my special treasure
on the day when I act.
I will spare them
as a father spares the son who serves him.
Then once more you will see the difference
between the righteous and the wicked,
between the one who serves God
and the one who does not serve him.

fields.title: Malachi 4
fields.body_html:
The day is coming

For see, the day is coming,
blazing like a furnace,
when all the arrogant and all evildoers will be stubble.
The day that is coming will set them on fire, says the LORD of Armies,
and leave them neither root nor branch.
But for you who revere my name, the sun of righteousness will rise,
bringing healing in its wings.
You will go out leaping like calves let out of the stall.

Remember the law of Moses

You will trample on the wicked;
they will be ashes
beneath your feet
on the day when I act,
says the LORD of Armies.

Remember the law of my servant Moses,
the statutes and rulings I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel.
See, I am sending you
Elijah the prophet
before the day of the LORD comes,
that great and terrible day.
He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children
and the hearts of children to their fathers,
so that I will not come
and strike the land with total destruction.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Remember the law of my servant Moses, the statutes and rulings I commanded him at Horeb for all Israel. See, I am sending you Elijah the prophet before the day of the LORD comes, that great and terrible day. He will turn the hearts of fathers to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, so that I will not come and strike the land with total destruction.

— Malachi 4:4–6

Malachi ends with two names. Moses stands for the law that God had given, which the people are told to remember. Elijah stands for the prophet who called Israel back to God on Mount Carmel, and who will come again before the great day. Between them they sum up everything the Old Testament has said: what God requires, and what God has promised to do. And the promise is about families, hearts turned toward one another, as if the healing of the nation had to begin at home.

The question the book leaves with you

Malachi was written for people who had not abandoned God but had grown weary of him. They still came to the temple, still offered sacrifices, still called themselves his people. But they gave him their leftovers, kept back what was his, broke faith with their wives, and said, “It is useless to serve God.” The book’s question is whether that weariness is ours. Do we still go through the motions while asking, under our breath, “In what way have you loved us?”

Malachi’s answer is not a new argument but a reminder. God has loved them. He does not change. He keeps a book of remembrance for those who fear him and talk with one another about him. And he is coming, both to refine and to heal.

Where it points

The silence after Malachi lasted some four hundred years. Then an angel told an old priest in the temple that his son would go ahead of the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah, to turn the hearts of fathers back to their children” (Luke 1:17). That son was John the Baptist, and Jesus said of him, “And, if you will receive it, John is Elijah, whose coming was foretold” (Matthew 11:14).

The Lord whom John prepared for came suddenly to his temple, and on a high mountain Moses and Elijah, the two names of Malachi’s last verses, “appeared before them, talking with Jesus”. When the disciples asked about Elijah coming first, Jesus answered both that “Elijah is indeed coming” and that “Elijah has come already” (Matthew 17:11–12). Christians have understood the promise as fulfilled in John, and some expect a further fulfilment before Christ returns. Jewish families still set a cup for Elijah at Passover. The book that closes the Old Testament leaves its door open.

Where to go from here

A few places in this library to take Malachi further:

  • On the God who does not change (3:6). Charles H. Spurgeon’s sermon The Immutability of God, on Malachi 3:6, and his Morning by Morning, November 2, on the same verse.
  • On the refiner’s fire (3:2–3). A. B. Simpson’s The Holy Spirit, or Power from on High, chapter “The Last Message of the Holy Ghost to the Old Dispensation”; Spurgeon’s Morning by Morning, October 15, on “But who may abide the day of his coming?”; The Key Teachings of Jeanne Guyon, an Ochorus Original, chapter “The Cross and the Refiner’s Fire”; and Hannah Whitall Smith’s The God of All Comfort, chapter “Things That Cannot Be Shaken”, which draws on Malachi 3:3–4 and 3:12.
  • On bringing the full tithe (3:8–12). Faithful with Little, an Ochorus Original, chapter “Firstfruits”.
  • On the messenger and Elijah (3:1; 4:5). A. W. Tozer’s sermon He Must Increase (John 3:30), and R. A. Torrey’s Three Fires (Matthew 3:11), both on John the Baptist.
  • On Malachi in the early church. Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho, chapter 117, on Malachi’s pure offering among the nations (1:11), and chapter 49, on Elijah as forerunner; and Augustine’s The City of God, Book XX, chapters 25 and 29, on Malachi’s prophecy of the judgement and the coming of Elijah.

And read the opening chapters of Mark and Luke in this same edition, where the messenger arrives.

Every reference to Malachi in this library can be tapped to read the verse. But the best next step may be to take to heart the promise made to those who talked with one another about the LORD, when most of their neighbours had given up:

They will be mine, says the LORD of Armies, my special treasure on the day when I act. I will spare them as a father spares the son who serves him.

— Malachi 3:17
